details:
**Denali (Mount McKinley)**
The highest peak in North America (about 20,310 feet), located in Denali National Park. Its Koyukon Athabaskan name means "the tall one" or "the high one"; it was officially called Mount McKinley after President William McKinley until a 2015 renaming restored Denali (the federal name was changed back to McKinley in 2025). A popular climbing route up it is the West Buttress, and nearby Mount Foraker is in the same park.

**Prudhoe Bay and the Trans-Alaska Pipeline**
Prudhoe Bay on the North Slope is the largest oil field in the United States. An 800-mile, largely above-ground pipeline carries its oil south to the ice-free port of Valdez on Prince William Sound. Oil revenue funds the Alaska Permanent Fund, which pays an annual dividend to every resident.

**Exxon Valdez oil spill**
In 1989 the oil tanker Exxon Valdez ran aground on Bligh Reef near Valdez in Prince William Sound, spilling roughly 11 million gallons of crude oil. It was one of the worst environmental disasters in U.S. history.

**Juneau**
The state capital, located in the southeastern Panhandle on the Gastineau Channel. It cannot be reached by road from the rest of North America and is accessed mainly by air or by the Alaska Marine Highway ferry system.

**Anchorage**
The state's largest city, on Cook Inlet near the Chugach Mountains. Its Ted Stevens International Airport is among the busiest cargo airports in the world, its Lake Hood is the world's busiest seaplane base, and it has a coastal trail named for governor Tony Knowles.

**Valley of Ten Thousand Smokes**
An ash-filled valley in Katmai National Park created by the 1912 eruption of Novarupta, the largest volcanic eruption of the 20th century. It was named for the thousands of fumaroles (steam vents) that rose from the ash flow after the eruption.

**Katmai National Park and Kodiak Island**
Katmai, centered on Mount Katmai, is famous for brown bears catching salmon. Kodiak Island, the second-largest island in the U.S., lies off the Alaska Peninsula, is home to the huge Kodiak bear, and was home to the Alutiiq people. Three Saints Bay on Kodiak was the site of the first Russian settlement in the region.

**Aleutian Islands**
A volcanic island chain stretching west toward Asia, including Unimak, Attu, Kiska, and the Islands of the Four Mountains. Japan occupied Attu and Kiska in World War II, and Dutch Harbor on Amaknak Island, once a military base, is now a major fishing port.

**Mount Shishaldin**
A volcano on Unimak Island in the Aleutians, often called the most symmetrical volcanic cone on Earth.

**Utqiagvik (Barrow) and the North Slope Borough**
Utqiagvik, formerly called Barrow, is the northernmost city in the U.S., on the Beaufort Sea near Point Barrow, the state's northernmost point. It is the seat of the North Slope Borough. Alaska is divided into boroughs instead of counties, and the vast Unorganized Borough covers more than half of the state.

**Iditarod Trail Sled Dog Race**
An annual long-distance dog sled race that starts in the Anchorage area and ends in Nome on Norton Sound by the Bering Sea, passing checkpoints such as Kaltag along the way.

**Yukon River**
One of the longest rivers in North America (often listed as the third longest). It flows west across the state and empties into the Bering Sea. The Kuskokwim River, which rises west of Mount Gerdine, is another major river.

**Wrangell-St. Elias National Park**
The largest national park in the United States by area. Alaska as a whole contains 17 of the 20 highest peaks in the U.S. Other national parks include Gates of the Arctic, Glacier Bay (a humpback whale habitat), Lake Clark (with the Chigmit Mountains and Dall sheep), and Kobuk Valley, whose sand dunes are the northernmost dune field in the U.S. and were studied by NASA as an analog for Mars.

**1964 Good Friday earthquake**
A magnitude 9.2 earthquake, the most powerful in North American recorded history. It caused tsunamis that hit Whittier, Kodiak, and Seward, and it destroyed much of the town of Valdez.

**Seward's Purchase and Russian America**
Alaska was explored by Vitus Bering's expedition, colonized by the Russian-American Company, and bought from Russia in 1867 by Secretary of State William Seward (critics called it "Seward's Folly"). The Tlingit fought the Russians at the Battle of Sitka in 1804, and a legacy of Russian rule is that Alaska has the highest share of Orthodox Christians of any U.S. state.
